title: The Earliest Moment When Everyone Become Friends
statement:
A social group has `n` people, numbered `0` to `n - 1`. Each entry `logs[i] = [timestamp, x, y]` records that people `x` and `y` became friends at time `timestamp`. The entries may appear in any order.

Friendship goes both ways. Two people are **acquainted** if they are friends, or if one of them is a friend of someone acquainted with the other; in other words, they are linked by a chain of friendships.

Return the smallest timestamp at which every person is acquainted with every other person. If that never happens after all the entries, return `-1`.
constraints: Each pair of people appears in at most one entry
notes:
## Intuition

Everyone is acquainted with everyone exactly when all `n` people sit in one connected group of the friendship graph. Adding friendships in time order can only merge groups, never split them, so the answer is the moment the number of groups first drops to one. A brute force would rebuild the graph and run a search after every entry, costing O(L · (n + L)). A union-find structure answers "are these two already in one group?" in near-constant time, so a single pass over the sorted entries is enough.

## Approach

1. Give every person their own group: `parent[i] = i`.
2. `find` follows parent links up to a group's root, halving the path as it goes so later lookups are faster.
3. Sort a copy of `logs` by timestamp into `ordered`, and set `groups = n`.
4. For each entry, find the roots of `x` and `y`. If they match, the two were already acquainted, so skip it.
5. Otherwise attach one root under the other and decrease `groups`.
6. When `groups` reaches 1, return this entry's `timestamp`. If the loop ends first, return `-1`.

## Example 1, step by step

The entries are already in time order and `groups` starts at 6. `20190101` joins 0 and 1 (5 groups), `20190104` joins 3 and 4 (4), `20190107` brings 2 to {3, 4} (3), and `20190211` brings 5 to {0, 1} (2). At `20190224`, 2 and 4 already share a root, so nothing changes. At `20190301`, 0 and 3 sit in different groups; merging them leaves one group, so the answer is `20190301`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(L log L) for the sort; the union-find work is nearly O(L) with path halving.
- Space: O(n + L) for `parent` and the sorted copy.

## Pitfalls

- The entries are not guaranteed to be in time order; skipping the sort gives wrong answers.
- Count merges, not entries: a friendship inside an existing group must not decrease `groups`.
- Return `-1` when the group count never reaches 1, for example when someone has no friends at all.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `parent` | parent link of each person; a root points to itself |
| `find` | returns the root of a person's group |
| `ordered` | the entries sorted by timestamp |
| `groups` | number of separate groups so far |
| `rootX`, `rootY` | roots of the two new friends' groups |

narration.2: Every person starts as the root of a group of their own.
narration.3: find returns the root of the group that a person belongs to.
narration.4: Climb parent links until reaching a root, which points to itself.
narration.5: Path halving: point this person at their grandparent so later lookups are shorter.
narration.8: The root identifies the whole group.
narration.10: Process the friendships in time order, since the entries may arrive shuffled.
narration.11: Before any friendship, there are n separate groups.
narration.12: Take the next friendship: its time and the two people involved.
narration.13: Find the group of the first person...
narration.15: Already in one group: this friendship connects nobody new.
narration.18: Merge the two groups by hanging one root under the other.
narration.20: A single group means everyone is acquainted with everyone.
narration.21: This is the earliest such moment, because entries are taken in time order.
narration.24: The friendships ran out with more than one group left, so the answer is -1.
